title: Async composition without the clock
description: The Task plumbing a web service lives on — caching the in-flight Task, first-SUCCESS hedged reads, strictly sequential pipelines, bridging callbacks with TaskCompletionSource, eager argument validation, selective failure funnels and TaskStatus snapshots. Every test is deterministic: pre-completed tasks and TaskCompletionSource drive completion order, never the wall clock. Nearest existing units: jstrain-cs 20/01 (cache-aside and the stampede), jstrain-cs 08/01-04 (await/WhenAll timing, cancellation, WhenAll aggregation + async void, async streams) — none of those are re-taught here.

exercises.title: Memoize the Task, not the result
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Your config loader is memoized, but under a cold-start burst the backing store still sees dozens of identical reads. Why, and what do you cache instead?"

**Contract.** `Once(factory)` returns a function. The FIRST time that function is called it invokes `factory()` and remembers the returned `Task<string>`; EVERY call — before the task completes and after — returns that same `Task` object. The factory therefore runs exactly once, even while its first task is still pending. (Single-threaded callers here; making it thread-safe is a module 09 topic.)

**Your task.** Implement the stubbed local function:
- `Func<Task<string>> Once(Func<Task<string>> factory)` → a function that starts the factory on its first call and hands every caller that same Task

**Worked example.** Two calls before anything completes → `ReferenceEquals(t1, t2)` is **true** and the factory ran **1** time.
exercises.explanation:
Caching a result can only happen after the result exists; until then, every caller misses and starts its own load (a cache stampede). The Task exists the instant the load starts, so caching it closes that window.

For `var t1 = f(); var t2 = f();` with a pending source:
- call 1: `cached` is null → `factory()` runs (calls = 1) → its Task is stored and returned
- call 2: `cached` is set → the same Task is returned → `ReferenceEquals(t1, t2)` is **true**, calls stays **1**

Sharing the in-flight Task turns N concurrent misses into one load and N awaiters.

The production caveat: a Task that FAULTED is shared just as faithfully, so after one failed load every later caller gets the same exception forever. Real code evicts the cached task when it faults (or caches it with a TTL) so the next caller retries.
hints: A Task is a handle you have before the work finishes — what if that handle is the thing you remember?
Capture a Task<string>? variable in the returned lambda; on first call assign factory() to it, then always return it (??= does both).
Store the Task itself in a captured variable on the first call and hand that same Task to every caller, so later callers await the in-flight work instead of starting it again

exercises.title: First replica to answer wins
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "p99 latency is dominated by one slow replica. You fire the read at two replicas — how do you return the first answer?"

**Contract.** Return the value of the first replica to complete SUCCESSFULLY. `Task.WhenAny(a, b)` completes with the first task to finish (a `Task<Task<string>>`) — but "finished" includes faulted, and a replica that answered with an exception has not answered. So when the first finisher faulted (or was canceled), the result is whatever the OTHER replica produces: its value, or, if it fails too, its exception. When both tasks are already complete at the call, `WhenAny` picks the first argument — the tests pin that.

**Your task.** Implement the stubbed local function:
- `async Task<string> FirstReadyAsync(Task<string> a, Task<string> b)` → the first successful replica's value; the second replica's exception only when both fail

**Worked example.** `a` pending, `b` completed with "b", then `a` completed → **"b"**.
exercises.explanation:
`WhenAny` answers "which one finished?"; it does not answer "which one succeeded?" — and a hedged read needs the second.

For `a.SetException(...)` before `b.SetResult("b")`:
- `await Task.WhenAny(a, b)` → the task `a` (the first to complete, faulted)
- `a.IsCompletedSuccessfully` is false → await the other replica instead
- `await b` → **"b"**

The naive `await await Task.WhenAny(a, b)` rethrows replica a's exception even though replica b answered a moment later — hedging that makes the p99 better and the error rate worse. In production also cancel the loser (a shared `CancellationTokenSource`) so its work stops, and observe its exception so it is not lost.
hints: WhenAny does not give you the string — look at its return type.
Task.WhenAny(a, b) is a Task<Task<string>> that completes with the first FINISHED task; check IsCompletedSuccessfully before trusting it, else await the other task.

WhenAny yields the first task to finish, which still has to be awaited for its value, and a finisher that faulted is not an answer, so fall back to awaiting the other replica and let only its failure surface

exercises.title: Validate eagerly: throw before the Task
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "`async Task<int> LoadAsync(string id) { if (bad) throw ...; await ...; }` — when does the caller see that exception? Fix it so argument errors surface at the call."

**Contract.** In an `async` method EVERY exception, even one thrown before the first await, is captured into the returned Task: the call itself never throws. Argument validation should be eager instead. `ParseAndLoadAsync` is a plain (non-async) method that parses `id` with the invariant culture and throws `ArgumentException` immediately when it is not an integer — before any Task is created and before `load` is called. A valid id is handed to a private `async` local function that awaits `load(parsed)` and returns its value.

**Your task.** Implement the stubbed local function (keep it non-async):
- `Task<int> ParseAndLoadAsync(string id, Func<int, Task<int>> load)` → validate, then `return LoadCore(parsed);` with a nested `async Task<int> LoadCore(int value)`

**Worked example.** `ParseAndLoadAsync("7", n => Task.FromResult(n * 10))` → **70**; `ParseAndLoadAsync("abc", …)` throws at the call.
exercises.explanation:
The `async` keyword turns a method body into a state machine whose exceptions land in the Task. Splitting the method moves validation outside that machine.

For `ParseAndLoadAsync("7", n => Task.FromResult(n * 10))`:
- the wrapper parses "7" → 7, no throw
- `LoadCore(7)` awaits `load(7)` → 70 → result **70**

For `"abc"`: `TryParse` fails and the wrapper throws right there — `Throws<ArgumentException>` sees it even though nobody awaited anything. Same rule the BCL follows: argument exceptions are thrown eagerly, operational failures travel in the Task.
hints: Ask where an exception thrown inside an async method actually goes — into the call, or into the returned Task?
A non-async wrapper can throw synchronously; put the awaiting part in a nested async local function and return its Task.
Split the method in two, a plain wrapper that validates and throws immediately, then hands off to a private async local function that does the awaiting

exercises.title: Strictly one at a time, in order
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "This partner API rejects concurrent requests from one client. Load every id through it, results in the original order."

**Contract.** Start `fetch(id)` for the first id, await it, append the result, and only then start the next id. Results are in input order; an empty list yields an empty result and makes no calls. (Firing every fetch first and awaiting them together would be concurrent — exactly what this downstream forbids; the last test controls completion with `TaskCompletionSource` and checks that the second fetch starts only after the first finished.)

**Your task.** Implement the stubbed local function:
- `async Task<List<int>> LoadAllAsync(List<int> ids, Func<int, Task<int>> fetch)` → the fetched values in input order, each fetch started only after the previous one completed

**Worked example.** `[1, 2, 3]` with `fetch = id => id * 2` → **[2, 4, 6]**, called in order 1, 2, 3.
exercises.explanation:
An `await` inside a loop body suspends the loop itself, so the next iteration — and the next `fetch` — cannot begin until the current task has completed.

For `[1, 2, 3]` with `id => Task.FromResult(id * 2)`:
- iteration 1: fetch(1) → 2, appended
- iteration 2: fetch(2) → 4, appended
- iteration 3: fetch(3) → 6, appended → **[2, 4, 6]**

Sequential-by-construction is the correct answer when the callee forbids concurrency; reach for WhenAll only when it allows it.

(About the last test: it observes the second fetch starting synchronously inside `gates[0].SetResult(10)`, because an `await` continuation runs inline on the completing thread when there is no `SynchronizationContext` and the source was not created with `RunContinuationsAsynchronously`. That holds in this console harness; under a UI or legacy ASP.NET context the continuation would be posted instead, so a test written this way is environment-sensitive.)
hints: Where the await sits decides whether calls overlap — inside the loop, or after starting them all?
foreach (var id in ids) results.Add(await fetch(id)); — each await finishes before the loop advances.
Loop over the ids and await each fetch inside the loop body before the next iteration starts, appending each answer so results keep the input order

exercises.title: Bridge a callback into a Task
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "This SDK only offers `OnMessage(Action<string> handler)`. Expose it as `Task<string> NextMessageAsync()`."

**Contract.** Create a `TaskCompletionSource<string>`, call `subscribe` exactly once with a handler that completes it, and return `tcs.Task` immediately (still pending until the event fires). The first message completes the task; later messages must be ignored without throwing — use `TrySetResult`, because `SetResult` throws on a second completion. (`TaskCreationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously` is a good habit so awaiters do not run inside the SDK's callback; it is not asserted.)

**Your task.** Implement the stubbed local function:
- `Task<string> NextMessageAsync(Action<Action<string>> subscribe)`

**Worked example.** Fire "first" then "second" → the task's result is **"first"**.
exercises.explanation:
A TaskCompletionSource is a Task whose completion you control by hand — the bridge from push (callbacks) to pull (await).

For two events "first" then "second":
- `subscribe` received `msg => tcs.TrySetResult(msg)`
- "first" → `TrySetResult` succeeds → the task completes with "first"
- "second" → `TrySetResult` returns false, nothing throws → result stays **"first"**

Always complete a TaskCompletionSource with the Try- variants when the event source can fire more than once.
hints: You need a Task you can finish yourself, from inside someone else's callback.
new TaskCompletionSource<string>(); subscribe(msg => tcs.TrySetResult(msg)); return tcs.Task.
A TaskCompletionSource turns a push callback into an awaitable pull, complete it from inside the handler with the try-variant so a second event cannot throw

exercises.title: Catch the expected failure only
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Code review: `try { ... } catch (Exception) { return null; }` around a repository call. What is wrong, and what should it look like?"

**Contract.** Await `load()`. On success return `(true, value, "")` — an empty string is still a successful value. When it throws `InvalidOperationException` (the one EXPECTED failure in this domain), return `(false, "", ex.Message)`. Every other exception type must propagate unchanged: catching it would turn a bug into a silent "not found".

**Your task.** Implement the stubbed local function:
- `async Task<(bool Ok, string Value, string Error)> TryLoadAsync(Func<Task<string>> load)` → the soft tuple for success and for the one expected failure; every other exception escapes unchanged

**Worked example.** A loader throwing `new InvalidOperationException("boom")` → **(false, "", "boom")**; one throwing `ArgumentException` escapes.
exercises.explanation:
A catch clause is a statement about which failures you understand. Naming exactly one type keeps every other failure visible.

For a loader that throws `new InvalidOperationException("boom")`:
- `await load()` throws inside the `try`
- the `catch (InvalidOperationException ex)` clause matches → **(false, "", "boom")**

An `ArgumentException` does not match that clause, so it leaves the method — and the caller's logs show a real bug instead of a quiet "Ok = false". Catch what you can handle; let the rest fly.
hints: Which exceptions are outcomes your caller should branch on, and which are bugs that must stay loud?
Wrap the await in try; catch only InvalidOperationException and build the soft tuple from ex.Message.
Catch only the one exception type that is an expected outcome and translate it into the soft tuple, letting every other exception fly so real bugs stay loud

exercises.title: Health endpoint: describe a Task
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "The `/health` endpoint says `warmup: done` whenever `task.IsCompleted` — even when warm-up crashed. Fix the status mapping."

**Contract.** Map a Task to one word: `"ok"` when it completed successfully, `"failed"` when it faulted, `"canceled"` when it was canceled, and `"pending"` otherwise. `IsCompleted` is true for ALL three terminal states, which is why `IsCompletedSuccessfully` exists — check the specific flags.

**Your task.** Implement the stubbed local function:
- `string Describe(Task t)` → `IsCompletedSuccessfully` → "ok", `IsFaulted` → "failed", `IsCanceled` → "canceled", else "pending"

**Worked example.** `Task.FromException(new InvalidOperationException("x"))` → **"failed"** (its `IsCompleted` is true).
exercises.explanation:
A Task has one success ending and two failure endings; `IsCompleted` only tells you it ended.

For `Task.FromException(new InvalidOperationException("x"))`:
- `IsCompletedSuccessfully` → false
- `IsFaulted` → true → **"failed"**

Reading the specific terminal flag (or `t.Status`) is the difference between a health check and a health lie.
hints: IsCompleted answers "did it end?", not "did it succeed?".
Test IsCompletedSuccessfully, then IsFaulted, then IsCanceled; anything else has not finished.
Check the specific terminal flags in order, successful completion first, then faulted, then canceled, and treat anything not yet completed as pending — plain IsCompleted is true for all three endings
